prompts.question: Evaluate the success of these campaigns in reducing the incidence of cervical cancer in Australian women. Include reference to the data in your answer.
markerNotes: The top rows need a judgement about success and the evidence for it: name the years and rates from the graph, then say what the data can and cannot show.
Separate the screening program from the vaccine programs. The graph's annotations allow a sentence on each, and an answer that treats them as one loses the comparison.
Correlation is not proof. An answer that says the program caused the fall must say what else might have changed, or it is a claim and not an evaluation.
commonStudentErrors: Says the campaigns caused the decline without noting that incidence was already falling before the screening program began.
Quotes the graph without judging success, so the answer describes the data and does not evaluate it.
Treats the vaccination programs as shown to have reduced incidence, when the graph shows no clear drop after 2007.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Provides an extensive evaluation of the success of the campaigns on the incidence of cervical cancer based on a detailed analysis of the stimulus; Provides a well-informed judgement as to the success of the campaigns
5 marks: Provides a thorough evaluation of the success of campaigns on the incidence of cervical cancer based on an analysis of the data; Provides an informed judgement as to the success of the campaigns
4 marks: Provides an evaluation of the success of campaigns on the incidence of cervical cancer with reference to the data; Provides a judgement
2-3 marks: Provides some points about the effect of the campaign(s) on the incidence of disease; Makes link(s) to the data
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
The national screening program that started in 1991 is followed by a large drop in the incidence of the disease, to about half, and therefore appears to have been effective in preventing the disease. However, it is not possible from these numbers to imply that the program was the cause of the drop as other factors may have changed concurrently. Also, incidence was dropping before 1991 and this decrease may have continued without the program.
Because human papillomavirus (HPV) causes most cervical cancers, vaccinating young girls against HPV could be an effective strategy for disease prevention in addition to screening. A program that includes vaccination of the whole population including boys will reduce the circulating viral load and is expected to add to the effectiveness. However, the data do not show a reduction in the incidence of cervical cancer since the beginning of these vaccination programs. This could be because the screening program is already very effective, or because the vaccines are delivered to young, school aged students and cervical cancer is likely to develop over several years and become evident in older women. Although it is expected that the incidence will reduce as a greater proportion of the total population is vaccinated, the effectiveness of each campaign separately cannot be assessed from these data.
The data show it is likely that public health programs are effective for preventing disease but they need to be continued for many years as well as studied separately before the effects can be properly assessed.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row with an extensive evaluation of the screening and vaccination campaigns, using the graph's values and dates, and a judgement that the data suggest effectiveness but cannot prove it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Incidence fell from about 13 per 100 000 women in 1994 to about 8 by 2000, a period that follows the screening program, which suggests the program may have been effective. However, the graph cannot show that the program caused the fall, and there is no clear drop after the vaccination programs began.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by making a point about the screening program and linking it to the data, with a tentative judgement. It does not weigh the vaccination programs separately or note that the decline began before 1991.

sampleAnswers.answer: The campaigns were a success because cervical cancer went down.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about the change in incidence. It makes a judgement with no data, no link to the graph and no reasoning about the campaigns.

prompts.scenario: The incidence of cervical cancer in the Australian population is shown in the graph from 1985−2015. Public health campaigns commenced during this period to reduce the incidence of cervical cancer. This included a national screening program to detect pre-cancerous cells and a vaccination program against human papillomavirus (HPV) which causes most cervical cancers. [Line graph titled by its axes: vertical axis 'Incidence of cervical cancer per 100 000 women' from 6 to 16; horizontal axis 'Year' from 1985 to 2015. Values read from the graph are approximate: about 14.7 in 1985, about 13.5 in 1990, about 13 in 1994, about 8.8 in 1997, about 8 in 2000, and between about 6.8 and 7.5 from 2002 onward, ending at about 6.9 in 2015. Annotations: arrow at 1991 'National screening program for women aged 20–69 years'; arrow at 2007 'HPV vaccine program for girls'; arrow at 2013 'HPV vaccine program for boys'. Source line: Adapted from National Cancer Control Indicators, https://ncci.canceraustralia.gov.au/ With permission from Cancer Australia.]
prompts.hscSection: Section II Answer Booklet 80 marks Attempt Questions 21–32 Allow about 2 hours and 25 minutes for this section

dotPoints.description: Use examples of infectious diseases to classify infectious agents as macroorganisms, microorganisms or non-cellular pathogens

prompts.question: Why is *Varroa* mite infection considered to be an infectious disease?
markerNotes: The top row justifies why Varroa mite infection counts as an infectious disease, by identifying the mite as a pathogen that can pass between organisms. The 1-mark row gives a correct fact about the mite, such as that it is a parasite, without tying it to infection.

NESA's sample calls the mite a parasitic pathogen that is spread between bees and hives that come into direct contact. Accept an equivalent justification drawn from the stimulus, such as the mite being an external parasite that moves between colonies.
commonStudentErrors: States that Varroa mite is a pest, without saying it is a pathogen that can be transmitted.
Restates the stimulus that the mite is the most serious pest of honey bees, which does not justify the infectious disease classification.
Gives a reason that is not about infection, such as the mite's size or appearance.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Provides justification for Varroa mite infection being an infectious disease
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer: *Varroa* mite is an infectious disease because the mite is a parasitic pathogen that is spread between bees and hives that come into direct contact with the pest.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by providing justification for Varroa mite infection being an infectious disease. It describes the mite as 'a parasitic pathogen' that is 'spread between bees and hives'.

sampleAnswers.answer: *Varroa* mite is a parasite that lives on honey bees.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information: 'a parasite that lives on honey bees' is accurate but does not say why the infection is infectious. Explaining that the mite is a pathogen that spreads between bees would lift it.

prompts.scenario: The *Varroa* mite is an external parasite of European honey bees and is considered to be the most serious pest of honey bees worldwide.
prompts.hscSection: Section II (80 marks). Allow about 2 hours and 25 minutes for this section.

dotPoints.description: Describe the adaptive features of prions, viruses, bacteria, protozoans, fungi and macroparasites

prompts.question: Describe a feature that distinguishes a viral from a bacterial pathogen.
markerNotes: The 2-mark row needs one feature that distinguishes a bacterium from a virus, stated as a comparison.
The feedback credits responses that compare one distinguishing feature, rather than only listing features of each pathogen.

NESA's sample compares size, with a bacterium at 1 to 10 micrometres and a virus at 0.05 to 0.1 micrometres; accept any answer NESA lists, such as cell structure (a prokaryotic cell compared with nucleic acids and a protein coat) or reproduction (binary fission compared with use of host cells).
commonStudentErrors: Lists features of a bacterium and of a virus separately, without comparing one distinguishing feature.
Gives a vague difference, such as 'bacteria are more complicated', instead of a specific feature such as cell structure or size.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Provides a feature that can be used to distinguish a bacterium from a virus
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer: The size of a bacterium is 1–10µm, a virus is 0.05–0.1µm so a bacterium is much larger than a virus.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by providing a feature that can be used to distinguish a bacterium from a virus. 'a bacterium is much larger than a virus' states the difference as a comparison.

sampleAnswers.answer: Bacteria and viruses are both pathogens that can cause disease in humans.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information, but 'both pathogens that can cause disease in humans' describes what the two share rather than a feature that distinguishes them. Naming a feature only one of them has, such as a cell structure or the way each one reproduces, would lift it.

prompts.hscSection: Section II (80 marks). Allow about 2 hours and 25 minutes for this section.

prompts.question: Outline an adaptation in a pathogen that facilitates transmission between hosts.
markerNotes: The top row needs an adaptation that moves the pathogen from one host to another, linked explicitly to that transfer. The 1-mark row names a feature that helps the pathogen inside the host without any link to transmission.

NESA's sample uses spores released after the fungus colonises a host, which then infect a new host. NESA's feedback also gives cholera's toxin-driven diarrhoea, which releases bacteria into water, as an example of a correct answer, so an equivalent specific adaptation should be accepted.
commonStudentErrors: Describes an adaptation that helps the pathogen survive or multiply inside the host, rather than one that moves it to a new host.
Gives a general feature of pathogens, such as 'fungi can reproduce', instead of one specific adaptation.
Names an adaptation but does not say how it leads to the pathogen reaching a new host.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Outlines how a pathogen adaptation facilitates transmission between hosts
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer: After colonising a host, fungi can produce spores which can be released to infect a new host.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by outlining how a pathogen adaptation facilitates transmission between hosts. It links spore release to infection of a new host, through 'spores which can be released to infect a new host'.

sampleAnswers.answer: Fungi grow as thin threads called hyphae that spread through tissue inside the host.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information: 'spread through tissue inside the host' describes growth inside the host, which is the internal benefit the question does not ask for. Explaining how a feature moves the pathogen to a new host, such as spores carried away in water, would lift it.

prompts.hscSection: Section II (80 marks). Allow about 2 hours and 25 minutes for this section.

dotPoints.description: Compare direct contact, indirect contact and vector transmission of pathogens that facilitate entry into and transmission between hosts

prompts.question: Outline ONE way that a pathogen can pass from person to person.
markerNotes: The mark needs one named route of transmission, described as it happens: what carries the pathogen and how it reaches the next person.
Answer with one way only. A second way adds nothing and can hide a weak first answer.
commonStudentErrors: Names a disease instead of a route, for example "through influenza".
Gives a route that needs another organism, such as a mosquito bite, which is vector transmission and not person-to-person spread.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Outlines ONE way that a pathogen can pass between hosts
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer: Viral particles emitted by one person can be transferred directly through the air and inhaled by another person.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by outlining a direct route of transmission through the air, with the pathogen carried in particles and inhaled. Naming a second route would not raise the mark.

sampleAnswers.answer: Through contact between people.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about person-to-person spread. It names no route or mechanism, so the outline the 2-mark row asks for is missing.

prompts.hscSection: Section II Answer Booklet 80 marks Attempt Questions 21–32 Allow about 2 hours and 25 minutes for this section

dotPoints.description: Conduct a laboratory experiment to assess the effect of antimicrobial treatment on the growth of microorganisms found in food or water

prompts.question: Outline an experimental procedure that could be used to determine if the pathogen is viral or bacterial.
markerNotes: The 2-mark row sketches a method, in general terms, that could separate a bacterial pathogen from a viral one.
The feedback names outlining the expected results for each pathogen as an area to improve, so the method should say what each pathogen would show.

NESA's sample uses an agar culture, on which bacteria grow and viruses do not, and light microscopy, which can show bacteria but not viruses; NESA also lists antibiotic treatment, which kills bacteria but not viruses, as an acceptable method.
commonStudentErrors: Describes a procedure but does not state the result expected for a bacterial pathogen and for a viral pathogen.
Describes a general test of the water or food without naming a method, such as agar culture or antibiotic treatment, that separates bacteria from viruses.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Sketches in general terms a method that can be used to distinguish between bacterial and viral pathogens
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer: The presence of a bacterial pathogen could be identified by using an agar culture. A viral pathogen cannot be cultured on agar. A bacterial pathogen can be observed using a high-powered light microscope, but a viral pathogen would not be able to be observed as it is too small.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by sketching in general terms a method, 'using an agar culture', that can distinguish bacterial from viral pathogens. 'A viral pathogen cannot be cultured on agar' gives the expected result for the viral pathogen.

sampleAnswers.answer: Put a sample of the water under a microscope and see what is present.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information, 'Put a sample of the water under a microscope', but it does not say what would be seen for each type of pathogen. Stating the expected result for a bacterial and a viral pathogen, such as bacteria visible under a light microscope and viruses too small to see, would lift it.

prompts.scenario: A waterborne disease outbreak occurred after a flood.
prompts.hscSection: Section II (80 marks). Allow about 2 hours and 25 minutes for this section.

prompts.question: A scientist wants to test the effectiveness of Jelly Bush honey using agar plates. Design a safe procedure that the scientist could use in a laboratory to investigate the effectiveness of Jelly Bush honey as a pharmaceutical to inhibit bacterial growth.
markerNotes: The 5-mark row needs a procedure someone could carry out: sterile agar plates, bacteria spread evenly, a honey disc and a control disc, incubation, then measurement of the clear zone.
Name the independent variable (the honey), the dependent variable (diameter of the zone of inhibition) and the constants (temperature, incubation time, bacterial strain, disc size).
Safety and repetition are separate marks in the top row. A sound procedure with neither loses them.
commonStudentErrors: Leaves out a control, so the honey's effect cannot be separated from the effect of the disc or the agar.
Gives a procedure with no safety steps, such as gloves, sealing the plates or disposing of the cultures.
Measures growth without saying how or when it is measured, or without repeating the trial.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Provides a logical procedure to test the effectiveness of Jelly Bush honey as an inhibitor of bacterial growth; Provides independent variable, dependent variable, variables kept constant and the use of a control; Includes appropriate safety considerations; Includes repetition
4 marks: Provides a logical procedure to test the effectiveness of Jelly Bush honey as an inhibitor of bacterial growth; Provides most of the features of a safe valid investigation such as – independent variable, dependent variable, variables kept constant and the use of control; – includes repetition
3 marks: Provides a procedure to test the effectiveness of Jelly Bush honey as an inhibitor of bacterial growth; Provides some features of a valid investigation
2 marks: Provides some features of a relevant investigation
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
1. Select appropriate safety equipment including gloves and safety clothing.
2. Prepare three nutrient agar plates, using sterile techniques. Seal one plate and label as control.
3. Inoculate the remaining plates with bacteria to cover the agar surface.
4. Place a sterile paper disc soaked in distilled water in the middle of an agar plate. Seal and label as Water.
5. Place a sterile paper disc soaked in Jelly Bush honey in the middle of an agar plate. Seal and label as Honey.
6. Incubate the plates at 25°C for 48 hours.
7. Remove from incubator but do not open any of the plates after incubation.
8. Observe the control plate to check for any contaminating bacteria.
9. For each agar plate, measure the zone of inhibition from edge to edge.
10. Repeat the experiment three more times and calculate an average.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row with a logical procedure, the variables, a control, safety steps and repetition. The printed sample also deals with contamination of the control plate.

sampleAnswers.answer: Prepare agar plates and spread bacteria evenly across them. Place a paper disc soaked in Jelly Bush honey on one plate and a disc soaked in water on another as a control. Incubate the plates and measure the clear zone around each disc.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row with a workable procedure that has a control. It does not name the constant variables, does not mention safety, and does not include repetition, so it stays in the middle band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Put some of the honey on the bacteria and see whether they die.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about testing honey against bacteria. It has no control, no measurement and no safety steps, so it is not a valid investigation.

prompts.scenario: Jelly Bush honey has been used by Aboriginal Peoples to treat cuts, sores and burns. Recent studies have shown that Jelly Bush honey has a very high level of methylglyoxal which is known to help fight infection.
prompts.hscSection: Section II Answer Booklet 80 marks Attempt Questions 21–32 Allow about 2 hours and 25 minutes for this section

dotPoints.description: Distinguish between innate and adaptive immune response

prompts.question: With reference to innate and adaptive immunity, explain how the body responds after exposure to *Helicobacter pylori*.
markerNotes: The top row needs an extensive account of both the innate and adaptive responses, including phagocytosis, the inflammatory response, and the stimulation and roles of B and T cells, all related to H. pylori.
NESA's sample moves from inflammation and phagocytes to antigen presentation and the activation of T and B cells, then to antibodies and memory cells, and ends by linking the two responses.
The feedback asks for a well-structured response that uses the three lines of defence and links the innate and adaptive responses, so markers should reward an explicit link.
The criteria do not require suppressor T cells, which the sample mentions, so markers should not require them.
commonStudentErrors: Describes the innate and adaptive responses as two separate lists without linking how they work together against H. pylori.
Describes the immune response in general terms without applying it to the gut infection in the stimulus.
prompts.markingCriteria:
7 marks: Demonstrates an extensive understanding of the innate and adaptive immune response including phagocytosis, inflammatory response, stimulation and role of B and T cells; Relates body’s responses to innate and adaptive immunity against H.pylori
5-6 marks: Demonstrates a thorough understanding of the innate and adaptive immune response including phagocytosis, inflammatory response, stimulation and role of B and T cells
3-4 marks: Demonstrates a sound understanding of the innate and adaptive immune response
2 marks: Demonstrates some understanding of the immune response
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
Damaged cells cause chemicals to be released, causing inflammation. Dilation of blood vessels as a part of inflammatory response increases blood flow which facilitates movement of phagocytes including macrophages and neutrophils into the infected area. Phagocytes process bacterial antigens and present them to the helper T-cells which triggers the adaptive immune response through release of cytokines. This results in activation of T and B cells. Cytotoxic T-cells specific to *H.pylori* directly attack the bacteria while the memory T-cells stay in the system to induce a rapid secondary immune response. Suppressor T-cells help with the regulation of the immune response. Plasma B-cells produce antibodies specific to *H.pylori* while memory B-cells remain in the system for secondary immune response. The antibodies can neutralise the antigens directly or tag it for destruction by phagocytes.

Both innate and adaptive immune responses work together to eliminate *H.pylori*. Innate response is rapid and provides immediate defence against *H.pylori* whereas adaptive response is slow but provides lifelong immunity through specific memory cells.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 7-mark row by demonstrating an extensive understanding of the innate and adaptive immune response, including phagocytosis, inflammatory response, stimulation and role of B and T cells, and relating these responses to immunity against H. pylori. 'Phagocytes process bacterial antigens and present them to the helper T-cells' links phagocytosis to T cell stimulation, and 'Plasma B-cells produce antibodies specific to H.pylori' relates the adaptive response to this infection.

sampleAnswers.answer: Macrophages and neutrophils, which are phagocytes, engulf *H. pylori* bacteria in the gut lining as part of the inflammatory response. The bacteria's antigens activate helper T cells and B cells, and the B cells produce antibodies against *H. pylori*. Memory cells remain afterwards for a faster response next time.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3–4 mark row by demonstrating a sound understanding of the innate and adaptive immune response, since 'Macrophages and neutrophils, which are phagocytes, engulf H. pylori bacteria' covers the innate response and 'the B cells produce antibodies against H. pylori' covers the adaptive one. It never explains that phagocytes present antigens to helper T cells, which then stimulate B cells, and explaining that link would lift it to the 5–6 mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: White blood cells called phagocytes come to the infection and destroy the bacteria. Antibodies are also made to fight the bacteria.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by demonstrating some understanding of the immune response, since 'phagocytes come to the infection and destroy the bacteria' describes one part of the response. 'Antibodies are also made' is not linked to the cells that make them or to the inflammatory response, so naming both would lift it.

prompts.scenario:
*Helicobacter pylori* is a bacterium that invades the gut lining and can cause damage to the stomach as shown in the diagram.

Stimulus: Diagram of a circular cross-section of the gut wall. Folds of the gut lining are drawn as dotted outlines, with darker grey shading in the tissue around them. Labels: 'Gut lining' at top left, pointing to the outer edge of the folds; 'Inflammatory cells' at lower left, pointing to the shaded tissue; 'Mucus' on the right, pointing to a pale band; and '*Helicobacter pylori*' on the right, pointing to small dark bacteria scattered in the mucus beside the lining.

scenarioImage.alt: Diagram of a gut wall cross-section with Helicobacter pylori bacteria in the mucus beside the gut lining.

dotPoints.description: Interpret and construct diagrams of the innate immune system including barriers, secretions, phagocytic leukocytes, antimicrobial proteins, inflammatory response and fever

prompts.question: Describe how phagocytes help protect against pathogens.
markerNotes: The 2-mark row needs a clear description of what phagocytes do to a pathogen, not only a statement that they fight infection.
NESA's sample gives two steps in order: the phagocyte engulfs or encloses the pathogen, then breaks it down.
Accept 'antigen' as well as 'pathogen' for the material taken in, since NESA's sample uses 'pathogen/antigen'.
commonStudentErrors: Describes the action of phagocytes in general words, without the precise terms 'engulf' or 'enclose'.
Says that phagocytes are white blood cells without describing what they do to a pathogen.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Provides a clear description of how phagocytes help protect against pathogens
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer: They engulf or enclose a pathogen/antigen as it can identify non-self-substances. Once the pathogen is engulfed, the phagocyte breaks down the pathogen or antigen.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing how phagocytes help protect against pathogens in two steps. 'They engulf or enclose a pathogen/antigen' gives the first step, and 'the phagocyte breaks down the pathogen or antigen' gives the second.

sampleAnswers.answer: Phagocytes are white blood cells that attack pathogens in the body.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information, as 'white blood cells that attack pathogens' is correct but says nothing about how the phagocyte deals with the pathogen. Explaining how the phagocyte engulfs the pathogen and then breaks it down would lift it.

prompts.hscSection: Section II (80 marks). Allow about 2 hours and 25 minutes for this section.

dotPoints.description: Conduct a scientific investigation to determine the effect of temperature on the viability of a non pathogenic E. coli

prompts.question: Describe the independent variable, the dependent variable and one controlled variable for this investigation.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 12 student plans to investigate the viability of a non-pathogenic laboratory strain of E. coli after incubation at different temperatures. Viability will be estimated by diluting the culture, spreading samples on nutrient agar and counting the colonies that grow after 24 hours at 37 °C.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes temperature as the independent variable, colony count as the dependent variable, and a controlled variable with a reason
2 marks: Describes the independent and dependent variables correctly but omits a controlled variable
1 mark: Identifies one variable in the investigation without describing its role
markerNotes: Strong answers define each variable in terms of this investigation, such as colony count as the measure of viability.
Credit a controlled variable with a reason, such as incubation time, which must be kept the same so that the comparison is fair.
Do not credit the colony count as the independent variable, because the student does not change it.
commonStudentErrors: Names the number of colonies as the independent variable, reversing the roles of the variables.
Lists a controlled variable without saying why it must be kept the same.
Names the culture itself as the controlled variable, which is not a variable that is held constant.

sampleAnswers.answer: The independent variable is the temperature at which the E. coli culture is incubated, which the student deliberately changes. The dependent variable is the viability, measured as the number of colonies counted on the agar plates. A controlled variable is the incubation time, which must be kept the same for every temperature so that any difference in colony count is due to temperature.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: all three variables are described for this investigation, and the controlled variable is justified.

sampleAnswers.answer: The independent variable is temperature and the dependent variable is the number of colonies.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: the independent and dependent variables are correct, but no controlled variable is given.

sampleAnswers.answer: The dependent variable is the colony count.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: identifies one variable without describing the logic of the investigation.

prompts.question: Construct a method for this investigation, including the temperatures tested, the number of replicates and one safety precaution for handling the culture.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: The student has a broth culture of the non-pathogenic E. coli, a water bath, a thermometer, sterile nutrient agar plates, sterile saline for dilutions, an incubator set to 37 °C and a supply of disinfectant. The investigation will test a range of temperatures, and each temperature will be repeated.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Constructs a complete, logical method with a suitable temperature range, replicates, timing and a relevant safety precaution
5 marks: Constructs a sound method with a range of temperatures, replicates and a clear sequence of steps
4 marks: Constructs a method with several relevant steps, including temperatures or replicates
3 marks: Describes a method with some relevant steps but omits replicates or the sampling procedure
2 marks: Identifies a relevant step, such as a temperature or a plating procedure, without a sequence
1 mark: Identifies a relevant safety or technique point without a method
markerNotes: Strong answers choose a temperature range that spans cold, mid and high temperatures, and say why those temperatures were chosen.
Credit replicates and a fixed incubation time, since these make results from different temperatures comparable.
Safety points should be specific to handling a bacterial culture, such as gloves, aseptic technique and autoclaving.
commonStudentErrors: Uses only one temperature, so no effect of temperature can be compared.
Omits replicates, so variation between cultures cannot be assessed.
Says the culture can be handled without gloves because it is non-pathogenic.

sampleAnswers.answer: Prepare a broth culture of the non-pathogenic E. coli and divide it into equal aliquots, one for each temperature. Incubate the aliquots at 4 °C, 20 °C, 37 °C and 50 °C, using a refrigerator, the bench and water baths checked with a thermometer. Hold each aliquot at its temperature for the same time, for example 60 minutes. Use three replicates at every temperature. After the set time, make serial dilutions of each aliquot in sterile saline, spread a sample of each dilution on nutrient agar, incubate the plates at 37 °C for 24 hours and count the colonies on plates with 30 to 300 colonies. Viability is estimated from the colony counts after incubation. Safety precaution: wear gloves and a lab coat, use aseptic technique, disinfect the bench, and autoclave all cultures and plates before disposal.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row: the method has a temperature range, replicates, a fixed time, a counting procedure and a specific safety precaution in a logical sequence.

sampleAnswers.answer: Use broth cultures at 4 °C, 20 °C, 37 °C and 50 °C, held for an hour. Spread samples on agar plates and incubate them at 37 °C, then count the colonies. Wear gloves when handling the culture.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row: several relevant steps are given, including temperatures, but there are no replicates and no dilution step.

sampleAnswers.answer: Incubate the culture at different temperatures, then count the colonies on agar plates.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: identifies relevant steps without a sequence or a specific temperature range.

dotPoints.description: Discuss the role of interleukin communication between innate and adaptive cells

prompts.question: Describe the role of interleukin-12 in linking an innate cell to a helper T cell during the response to a bacterial infection.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A patient has a bacterial infection in the lung. Dendritic cells at the infection site take up the bacteria and present bacterial antigen to naive helper T cells in a lymph node. During the infection, the dendritic cells and macrophages release interleukin-12 (IL-12).
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes IL-12 as released by innate cells and causing naive helper T cells to differentiate into Th1 cells, with a link to the response
2 marks: Describes IL-12 as a signal from an innate cell to a helper T cell with some accurate detail
1 mark: Identifies interleukin-12 or an innate cell without describing a role
markerNotes: Strong answers say which cell releases IL-12, which cell it acts on, and what that cell then does.
Credit the Th1 outcome, and the interferon-gamma that activates macrophages, as the link back to the infection.
Do not credit an answer that says IL-12 is released only by helper T cells.
commonStudentErrors: Says that interleukin-12 is released by helper T cells, which reverses the signal described.
Describes IL-12 as killing the bacteria directly, rather than as a signal.
Says the lymph node is where the bacteria are destroyed by interleukin-12.

sampleAnswers.answer: Dendritic cells and macrophages, which are innate cells, release interleukin-12 when they detect bacteria. IL-12 binds to naive helper T cells that have received antigen from a dendritic cell, signalling them to differentiate into Th1 helper T cells. These Th1 cells then release interferon-gamma, which activates macrophages to destroy the bacteria.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: IL-12 is linked from an innate cell to a helper T cell, with the Th1 outcome and its link to the infection.

sampleAnswers.answer: Interleukin-12 is released by macrophages and signals helper T cells to develop into Th1 cells.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: describes IL-12 as a signal from an innate cell to a helper T cell, but does not explain the outcome for the infection.

sampleAnswers.answer: Interleukin-12 is a chemical messenger.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: identifies IL-12 as a signalling molecule without describing its role in linking the cells.

prompts.question: Discuss how interleukin signals from innate cells can determine which type of helper T cell response develops in each patient.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Two patients have infections. Patient 1 has a bacterium that multiplies inside macrophages. Patient 2 has a large parasitic worm in the gut and surrounding tissue. Laboratory tests show high levels of interleukin-12 in the infected tissue of Patient 1 and high levels of interleukin-4 in the infected tissue of Patient 2.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Discusses how each interleukin drives a specific helper T cell response, links each response to the type of pathogen, and reaches a supported conclusion about the innate and adaptive link
5 marks: Discusses both interleukin signals and their helper T cell outcomes with mostly accurate links to the patients
4 marks: Discusses relevant signals and the type of response they produce, with some reasoning
3 marks: Identifies relevant signals with a limited link to the type of helper T cell response
2 marks: Identifies a relevant signal without explaining its role in the response
1 mark: Identifies an interleukin or an immune cell without further development
markerNotes: Strong answers name the helper T cell subtype each signal drives, such as Th1 for interleukin-12 and Th2 for interleukin-4.
Credit the link between each innate signal and the type of pathogen, rather than naming cytokines without a purpose.
Penalise answers that state the laboratory levels prove which cells released the interleukins.
commonStudentErrors: Says interleukins are produced only by helper T cells, ignoring their release by innate cells.
Describes interleukin-12 and interleukin-4 as having the same effect on helper T cells.
Assigns the wrong pathogen type to each helper T cell response.

sampleAnswers.answer: Interleukin-12 in Patient 1's tissue signals naive helper T cells to differentiate into Th1 cells. Th1 cells release interferon-gamma, which activates macrophages to destroy the bacteria inside them, so a cell-mediated response dominates. Interleukin-4 in Patient 2's tissue signals naive helper T cells to differentiate into Th2 cells. Th2 cells release interleukin-5 and interleukin-13, which activate eosinophils and support the antibody response, including IgE, which helps against large parasites. The innate signals therefore shape the adaptive response, so the helper T cell profile is matched to the type of pathogen. Because the signals act on naive helper T cells early in the infection, the innate response determines the direction of the adaptive response from its start. This shows that the innate and adaptive arms of immunity are linked, not separate. The evidence is consistent with this pattern, but laboratory levels alone cannot prove which cells released the interleukins.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row: both signals are linked to their helper T cell outcomes and to the type of pathogen, with a supported conclusion about the innate and adaptive link.

sampleAnswers.answer: Interleukin-12 from innate cells drives helper T cells towards Th1 responses, which activate macrophages against bacteria. Interleukin-4 drives helper T cells towards Th2 responses, which help against parasites. So the innate signals decide the type of adaptive response.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row: both signals and their outcomes are discussed with some reasoning, but the link to each patient is brief.

sampleAnswers.answer: Interleukin-12 and interleukin-4 are both released by immune cells.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: identifies relevant signals without explaining their role in the response.

dotPoints.description: Describe the roles of helper T cells, cytotoxic T cells, memory T cells and suppressor T cells of the cell-mediated immune response within the adaptive immune system

prompts.question: Describe the roles of cytotoxic T cells and suppressor T cells in the cell-mediated immune response to a virus that infects liver cells.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A virus infects liver cells in a patient. The infected cells display viral antigens on their surface, bound to MHC class I molecules. Once the infection is controlled, the patient's immune response must be reduced to prevent damage to healthy liver tissue.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes cytotoxic T cells killing infected cells and suppressor T cells limiting the response, with accurate mechanisms linked to the scenario
3 marks: Describes the roles of both cell types with some accurate detail
2 marks: Describes the role of one cell type with accurate detail
1 mark: Identifies a T cell type without describing its role
markerNotes: Strong answers name the mechanism for each cell type, such as perforin and granzymes for cytotoxic T cells and anti-inflammatory signals for suppressor T cells.
Credit a link to the scenario, such as recognising antigen on MHC class I molecules of infected liver cells.
Do not credit answers that describe the helper T cell or memory T cell roles as the answer to this question.
commonStudentErrors: Says cytotoxic T cells recognise antigen on MHC class II molecules, which mixes up the two pathways.
Describes suppressor T cells as the cells that kill infected cells.
Says suppressor T cells work only at the start of the infection rather than after it is controlled.

sampleAnswers.answer: In the cell-mediated immune response, cytotoxic T cells recognise viral antigen on the MHC class I molecules of infected liver cells, bind to them and release perforin and granzymes, which cause the infected cells to undergo apoptosis. Once the infection is controlled, suppressor T cells, also called regulatory T cells, release anti-inflammatory signals such as interleukin-10 and reduce the activity of cytotoxic T cells. This prevents excessive killing of healthy liver cells, so healthy tissue survives and the risk of autoimmune damage is reduced.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row: both cell types are described with accurate mechanisms and linked to the scenario of the infected liver cells.

sampleAnswers.answer: Cytotoxic T cells kill cells infected with a virus.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: describes the role of one cell type with accurate detail, but suppressor T cells are not described.

sampleAnswers.answer: Suppressor T cells are a type of T cell.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: identifies a T cell type without describing its role.

prompts.question: Analyse the consequences for this patient if suppressor T cells were not functioning, referring to the cell-mediated response described.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A patient with a viral liver infection has a cell-mediated response in which cytotoxic T cells are very active. The patient's suppressor T cells are not working because of a fault in their development. Blood tests show that the patient's liver enzymes are rising while the viral load is falling.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses the consequences of the missing suppressor activity for cytotoxic T cells, inflammation and healthy tissue, and explains the falling viral load in context
5 marks: Analyses the consequences for cytotoxic T cells and tissue damage with mostly accurate links to the scenario
4 marks: Describes consequences of the missing suppressor activity with some links to the blood test results
3 marks: Identifies a consequence of the missing suppressor activity with a limited link to the scenario
2 marks: Identifies a consequence without linking it to the blood tests
1 mark: Identifies the liver enzyme result without a consequence
markerNotes: Strong answers explain why a rising enzyme level indicates tissue damage, rather than just stating the result.
Credit the idea that the response still works, since the viral load falls, while its cost to healthy tissue increases.
Credit a reasoned link between the missing regulation and autoimmune risk, rather than a list of diseases.
commonStudentErrors: Says the rising liver enzymes show the virus is growing, rather than showing damage to liver cells.
Claims that suppressor T cells are needed to kill the virus.
Says the falling viral load shows the patient has no problem with the response.

sampleAnswers.answer: Without suppressor T cells, the cell-mediated response is not limited once the infection is under control, so the immune response continues unchecked. Cytotoxic T cells continue to bind and kill infected liver cells, and they cause bystander damage to nearby healthy liver cells, which explains the rising liver enzymes. Inflammation is also sustained, because suppressor T cells normally release interleukin-10 and other signals that dampen it. The consequences include severe liver damage and a higher risk of autoimmune reactions in which immune cells attack the patient's own tissues. The falling viral load shows the response is still effective, but its cost is increasing tissue damage to the liver, so the patient needs close monitoring and a medical review of the treatment plan. Without suppressor activity, the liver damage can also persist after the virus has been cleared.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row: the missing regulation is linked to cytotoxic activity, inflammation and tissue damage, and the falling viral load is explained in context.

sampleAnswers.answer: Cytotoxic T cells keep killing infected liver cells, so the liver is damaged. Suppressor T cells normally stop this, so the patient may get autoimmune damage. The rising liver enzymes show that liver cells are being damaged.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row: describes consequences with some links to the blood test, but the falling viral load is not discussed.

sampleAnswers.answer: Without suppressor T cells, the immune response would be stronger and might damage the liver.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: identifies a consequence without linking it to the blood test results.

dotPoints.description: Describe the roles of plasma cells, memory B cells and antibodies of the humoral immune response within the adaptive immune system

prompts.question: Explain how antibodies are produced in response to the entry of a pathogen.
markerNotes: The top row needs the response to follow the steps in order, from the pathogen's antigen being recognised to plasma cells producing antibodies, with the role of each cell stated.

NESA's sample traces that sequence in two paragraphs: the antigen is recognised as non-self, a specific B cell is activated and replicates into plasma cells, and the plasma cells produce antibodies specific to the antigen.

The feedback credits responses that distinguish the roles of antigen-presenting cells, helper T cells and plasma B cells, and it names separating the antibody-mediated response from the cell-mediated response as an area to improve.
commonStudentErrors: Describes the cell-mediated response, in which T cells act against infected cells, when the question asks about antibody production.
Gives the steps out of sequence, for example describing antibodies being made before the antigen binds to a B cell.
Mentions antibodies without saying that they are produced by plasma cells, which are plasma B cells.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Demonstrates a thorough understanding of the immune response to the entry of a pathogen
3 marks: Demonstrates a sound understanding of the immune response to the entry of a pathogen
2 marks: Demonstrates some understanding of the immune response to the entry of a pathogen
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
Pathogens carry protein markers (antigens), so that when it enters a body, it is recognised as non-self. The immune response is then activated to destroy the pathogen.

The antigen of the pathogen binds to the receptor of a B cell and activates it. This specific B cell replicates to form plasma cells. Plasma cells produce an antibody that is specific to the antigen.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by demonstrating a thorough understanding of the immune response to the entry of a pathogen. It sequences the steps, from 'The antigen of the pathogen binds to the receptor of a B cell' to 'Plasma cells produce an antibody that is specific to the antigen'.

sampleAnswers.answer: When a pathogen enters the body, the immune system recognises it as foreign. White blood cells then make antibodies that attach to the pathogen so it can be destroyed.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by showing some understanding, as 'White blood cells then make antibodies' gives the outcome but names no specific cell that makes them. Explaining that a B cell binding the antigen becomes a plasma cell that produces the antibodies would lift it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Antibodies are proteins that help the body fight pathogens.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information, as 'Antibodies are proteins' is correct but does not explain how antibodies are produced. Explaining how an antigen activates a B cell that becomes a plasma cell would lift it.

prompts.hscSection: Section II (80 marks). Allow about 2 hours and 25 minutes for this section.

prompts.question: Describe the role of X, Y and Z in the process of antibody production.
markerNotes: The top row correctly describes antibody production and correctly identifies X, Y and Z by cell type and role, such as helper T cells activating B cells that become plasma cells. The 3-mark row outlines the process but refers to the flow chart only loosely.

NESA's sample names X as helper T cells, Y as B lymphocytes and Z as plasma cells, and describes macrophages working with helper T cells to activate the B cells. Check each of X, Y and Z against those roles rather than against the exact wording.
commonStudentErrors: Rewrites the flow chart's arrows, such as 'X leads to Y', without naming what X, Y and Z are.
Names the wrong cell for one of X, Y or Z, or leaves out the helper T cells' activation of the B cells.
Starts at the antibody and skips antigen presentation and cell activation, so the sequence is incomplete.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Correctly describes the process of antibody production with correct reference to the role of X, Y and Z
3 marks: Outlines the process of antibody production with some reference to the flow chart
2 marks: Outlines a process of antibody production
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer: The tick bite transfers antigenic alpha-gal sugar molecules into the skin. Macrophages, together with Helper T cells (X), activate B-lymphocytes (Y). These cells grow and differentiate into either memory cells, when exposure occurs, or plasma cells (Z) which produce antibodies against the antigen.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by correctly describing antibody production with correct reference to the roles of X, Y and Z. It identifies 'Helper T cells (X)' and 'B-lymphocytes (Y)', then 'plasma cells (Z) which produce antibodies'.

sampleAnswers.answer: Once alpha-gal enters the body, the immune system responds by making antibodies. These antibodies then bind to the alpha-gal molecules.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by outlining a process of antibody production, with 'the immune system responds by making antibodies'. It names none of the cells in X, Y or Z, so naming them and their roles, such as helper T cells activating B lymphocytes, would lift it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Alpha-gal is a sugar molecule that the body can react to.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information: 'a sugar molecule that the body can react to' repeats the stimulus without describing antibody production. Describing what happens to the alpha-gal in the immune response would lift it.

prompts.scenario:
Alpha-gal syndrome (AGS) is a tick-borne allergy to red meat caused by tick bites. Alpha-gal is a sugar molecule found in most mammals but not humans, and can also be found in the saliva of ticks. The diagram shows how a tick bite might cause a person to develop an allergic reaction to red meat.

The flow chart shows the process of antibody production following exposure to alpha-gal.

Stimulus: Flow chart of antibody production after exposure to alpha-gal, with blank boxes X, Y and Z.
- 'Alpha-gal' box and 'Macrophage' box, with arrows joining and pointing down into box X.
- X → box Y.
- Y → arrow to the left → 'Memory cells'.
- Y → arrow to the right → box Z.
- Z → arrow down → 'Antibodies'.
X, Y and Z are blank boxes, labelled only by those letters.

prompts.question: Explain the role of memory cells in the immune response.
markerNotes: The top row explains how memory cells are created during the first exposure and how they act on re-exposure, linking the two. The 2-mark row outlines a role, such as remembering the pathogen, without explaining how the cells form or why they respond faster.

NESA's sample states that B cells create memory cells in response to a specific antigen, and that on re-exposure they quickly differentiate into plasma cells or cytotoxic T cells. Accept either product of memory cells on re-exposure, since NESA's sample names both.
commonStudentErrors: Describes what memory cells do on re-exposure but never says how they were created during the first exposure.
States that memory cells 'remember' the pathogen but does not link this to a faster or stronger response on re-exposure.
Says memory cells make antibodies on the first exposure, which mixes up their role with that of plasma cells.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains the role of memory cells in the immune response
2 marks: Outlines the role of memory cells
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer: Memory cells are created by B-cells in response to a specific antigen. Memory cells remain in the lymph nodes after the infection. On re-exposure to the antigen, these memory cells quickly differentiate into plasma cells or cytotoxic T-cells, which neutralise the pathogen more rapidly to prevent disease.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining the role of memory cells in the immune response. It explains creation, 'Memory cells are created by B-cells in response to a specific antigen', and their action on re-exposure, 'these memory cells quickly differentiate into plasma cells or cytotoxic T-cells'.

sampleAnswers.answer: Memory cells are made after an infection and stay in the body. They help the body respond to the same pathogen again.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by outlining the role of memory cells, with 'They help the body respond to the same pathogen again'. It does not say how the cells are created or why the response is faster, so explaining how B cells form them during the first exposure and how they quickly differentiate on re-exposure would lift it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Memory cells are a type of white blood cell in the immune system.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information: 'a type of white blood cell' defines the cells but gives no role in the immune response. Explaining what the memory cells do on re-exposure would lift it.

prompts.scenario:
Alpha-gal syndrome (AGS) is a tick-borne allergy to red meat caused by tick bites. Alpha-gal is a sugar molecule found in most mammals but not humans, and can also be found in the saliva of ticks. The diagram shows how a tick bite might cause a person to develop an allergic reaction to red meat.

Stimulus: Four-stage diagram with a body outline and a tick-and-skin inset.
1. 'Tick bite': an enlarged tick with alpha-gal dots in its saliva, entering the skin of the arm. Label: 'When a tick bites a human, it transfers alpha-gal through its saliva into the skin tissue.'
2. 'Immune response': Y-shaped antibodies bound to alpha-gal dots in the body. Label: 'The body makes antibodies against the invading alpha-gal molecule. These antibodies stay in the body, ready to attack at the next alpha-gal exposure.'
3. 'Meat trigger': a cut of meat with alpha-gal dots, and an antibody in an inset with an arrow pointing to the head. Label: 'When a person eats the meat of a mammal, the alpha-gal present triggers an immune response.'
4. 'Symptoms appear in 4–5 hours': labels on a body outline reading dizziness (brain), swelling of the lips, difficulty breathing (lungs), itchy rash, and vomiting (stomach/intestines).

dotPoints.description: Interpret and construct diagrams of the adaptive immune system to demonstrate how the cell-mediated and humoral components of the immune system respond after primary and secondary exposure to a pathogen

prompts.question: Describe the features of antibody production shown in the graph.
markerNotes: The top row describes at least two specific, distinct features that the graph shows for both exposures, such as the time each response takes to start and the height of each peak. The 1-mark row gives a general statement, such as that the body responds faster the second time, without a feature read from the curve.

NESA's sample compares the first and second exposures on timing and concentration: antibody production takes longer and produces a lower concentration on first exposure, and is quicker and higher on re-exposure. Accept any feature that is read directly from the curve for both exposures.
commonStudentErrors: Gives a broad generalisation, such as 'the immune system gets stronger', rather than a feature the graph shows.
Describes features of only one exposure, usually the second, and leaves out the first.
Repeats the labels 'Tick bite' and 'Meat eaten' instead of describing what the curve does after each.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Describes features of antibody production shown in the graph
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer: On first exposure to the alpha-gal sugar by the tick bite, antibody production takes longer and only a lower concentration of antibodies is produced. On re-exposure, antibodies are produced more quickly and a higher concentration is produced.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing features of antibody production shown in the graph. It contrasts the two exposures, with 'antibody production takes longer' on first exposure and 'antibodies are produced more quickly' on re-exposure.

sampleAnswers.answer: The graph shows that the body makes antibodies after the tick bite and again after eating meat.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information: 'the body makes antibodies after the tick bite and again after eating meat' repeats the labels without describing how the curve changes. Describing the time taken and the size of each peak, such as the second peak being higher, would lift it.

prompts.scenario:
Alpha-gal syndrome (AGS) is a tick-borne allergy to red meat caused by tick bites. Alpha-gal is a sugar molecule found in most mammals but not humans, and can also be found in the saliva of ticks. The diagram shows how a tick bite might cause a person to develop an allergic reaction to red meat.

An allergic reaction to alpha-gal sugar is similar to a secondary immune response.

Stimulus: Graph with no numerical scales, showing antibody concentration against time.
- Y-axis: 'Concentration of antibodies'.
- X-axis: 'Time' (arrow). Two arrows on the time axis: 'Tick bite' (early) and 'Meat eaten' (later).
- The curve is flat at zero from the axis until just after the tick bite. It rises to a small hump, about a quarter of the height of the later peak, then falls to a low trough at the 'Meat eaten' arrow, close to the baseline.
- It then rises steeply to the highest point on the graph, and falls to a plateau that stays well above the level of the first hump until the end of the line.

dotPoints.description: Distinguish between passive and active immunity

prompts.question: Describe how a person acquires active immunity, and how a newborn acquires passive immunity from its mother.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A health student is preparing a summary for a parenting class. The summary covers two people: an adult who has been vaccinated against measles, and a newborn baby whose mother is immune to measles from a childhood infection.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes active immunity as the body making its own antibodies and memory cells after antigen exposure, and passive immunity as antibodies received from another source
2 marks: Describes one type of immunity accurately, with a relevant example
1 mark: Identifies active or passive immunity without describing how it is acquired
markerNotes: Strong answers name the source of the antibodies in each case: the body's own response, or another person's antibodies.
Credit the placenta as the route for maternal IgG antibodies, since this is the example in the scenario.
Credit a statement that passive protection does not produce memory cells, as this explains why it is short-lived.
commonStudentErrors: Says the newborn makes its own antibodies against measles, which is active immunity.
Says that a vaccine gives passive immunity because antibodies are present afterwards.
Confuses antigen and antibody, describing the vaccine as the antibody that protects the person.

sampleAnswers.answer: Active immunity is acquired when the body is exposed to an antigen, through infection or vaccination, and produces its own antibodies and memory cells. Passive immunity is acquired when antibodies are received from another source, such as maternal IgG antibodies that cross the placenta to the newborn. The newborn's protection is immediate but short-lived, because it has no memory cells of its own.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: both types are described accurately, with the source of the antibodies and a relevant example.

sampleAnswers.answer: A vaccinated adult makes its own antibodies and memory cells after exposure to the vaccine antigen.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: describes active immunity accurately with a relevant example, but passive immunity is not described.

sampleAnswers.answer: The mother's measles antibodies are present in the baby.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: identifies a relevant fact without describing how the immunity is acquired.

prompts.question: Analyse why a patient who receives tetanus immunoglobulin after a dirty wound also needs a tetanus vaccine for long-term protection.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A patient who has never been immunised against tetanus receives an injection of tetanus immunoglobulin, which contains antibodies to tetanus toxin, after a deep puncture wound from a rusty nail. At the same visit, the patient is given a dose of tetanus toxoid vaccine in the other arm.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses how the immunoglobulin gives immediate passive protection and the vaccine gives active immunity with memory cells, and explains why only the active response gives long-term protection
5 marks: Analyses the difference between passive and active protection with mostly accurate reasoning about duration
4 marks: Describes passive and active protection with some reasoning about why both are used
3 marks: Identifies a difference between passive and active protection with limited reasoning
2 marks: Identifies one type of protection without linking it to the patient
1 mark: Identifies tetanus or the vaccine without explaining its role
markerNotes: Strong answers explain the timing difference: immediate protection from antibodies that already exist, and a delayed response that builds memory.
Credit an explanation that the immunoglobulin supplies antibodies but does not stimulate the patient's own immune system.
Do not credit a claim that the immunoglobulin gives lifelong protection.
commonStudentErrors: Says the immunoglobulin gives long-term protection because antibodies are present in the blood.
Says the vaccine works straight away, so the immunoglobulin is not needed.
Describes the tetanus toxoid vaccine as containing live bacteria that cause the disease.

sampleAnswers.answer: The tetanus immunoglobulin supplies antibodies to tetanus toxin that already exist, so passive immunity is immediate. This protection is needed because the bacterium Clostridium tetani may already be producing toxin in the wound. However, these antibodies break down over weeks, and the immunoglobulin does not stimulate the patient's own immune system, so no memory cells are formed. The tetanus toxoid vaccine contains an inactivated toxin that triggers active immunity, with the patient's B cells making antibodies and memory cells. The vaccine response takes days to weeks to develop, so the immunoglobulin provides cover in the meantime. Only the active response, with its memory cells, gives long-term protection against future exposure. The patient is therefore protected in the short term by the immunoglobulin and in the long term by the vaccine response, which is why both are given at the same visit.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row: the timing and duration of passive and active protection are analysed, with a clear reason why both are needed.

sampleAnswers.answer: Immunoglobulin gives immediate passive protection, but the antibodies break down over time. The vaccine causes the patient to make their own antibodies and memory cells, which gives long-term active immunity.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row: describes passive and active protection with a reason for using both, but does not explain why the timing matters.

sampleAnswers.answer: The immunoglobulin protects the patient straight away, but the vaccine is needed for longer protection.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: identifies one type of protection and the need for the vaccine, with limited reasoning.

dotPoints.description: Use data to demonstrate how vaccinations support adaptive immunity

prompts.question: Assess the use of vaccinations and the vaccination schedule. Use the data provided to support your answer.
markerNotes: The 5-mark row needs a comprehensive account of what a vaccine does, linked to the graph and the other stimulus information, and a judgement of the schedule.
The 4-mark row has a sound understanding with some reference to the graph, and a relevant judgement.

NESA's sample explains that a vaccine triggers an immune response with a form of the antigen that does not cause infection, reads the graph to show that more booster doses mean longer immunity, and judges the vaccinations effective.
The feedback asks for a judgement rather than a description of the graph, and for use of all the stimulus, including the 1953 introduction and the cases in people aged 65 and over.
commonStudentErrors: Describes the rise and fall of antibody levels after each dose without stating a judgement about the schedule.
Describes a vaccine vaguely, for example as something that 'makes you immune', without explaining that it introduces an antigen that triggers an immune response without causing infection.
Uses only the graph and ignores the other stimulus, such as the 1953 introduction or the cases in people aged 65 and over.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Demonstrates a comprehensive understanding of the use of vaccines and the vaccination schedule, with reference to the graph and provided information; Makes a judgement about the value of the vaccination schedule
4 marks: Demonstrates a sound understanding of the use of vaccines and the vaccination schedule, with some reference to the graph or provided information; Makes a relevant judgement
3 marks: Demonstrates some understanding of the use of vaccines and the vaccination schedule
2 marks: Demonstrates understanding of vaccination and/or vaccination schedules
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer: Vaccinations are used to initiate an immune response using a form of the pathogen/antigen that will not result in infection. From the graph, the more booster shots, the longer the period of time the person is considered immune. Cases occurring in people aged over 65 would be the result of not having a booster for a long time. The reduction in numbers of tetanus cases would suggest that vaccinations are effective while the recurring schedule ensures a person maintains immunity.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by demonstrating a comprehensive understanding of the vaccination schedule with reference to the graph, and making a judgement about it. 'the more booster shots, the longer the period of time the person is considered immune' uses the graph to support that judgement.

sampleAnswers.answer: Vaccines are given so that people become immune to diseases. The schedule has several doses, and the graph shows that antibody levels rise after each dose.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by showing some understanding of vaccines and the schedule, as 'antibody levels rise after each dose' describes the graph. It makes no judgement about the schedule and does not explain how a vaccine triggers an immune response; stating whether the schedule is effective and why would lift it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Tetanus is a disease that vaccines help to prevent.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing some relevant information, as 'vaccines help to prevent' tetanus, but it does not use the graph or the schedule. Explaining how the booster doses build immunity, with reference to the graph, would lift it.

prompts.scenario:
Tetanus vaccines were introduced in 1953 resulting in reduced case numbers. The majority of recorded cases occurred in people aged 65 and over. The graph shows the vaccination schedule for tetanus.

Stimulus: Line graph titled 'Recommended vaccination schedule'. The x-axis shows age at vaccination, in years, with ticks at 0.2, 0.5, 1.5, 4 and 13. The y-axis shows tetanus antibody level, in IU/mL, on a logarithmic scale labelled 0, 0.01, 0.10, 1.00 and 10.00. Five syringe symbols mark the doses: 1st at about 0.2 years, 2nd at about 0.5 years, 3rd at about 1.5 years, 4th at about 4 years and 5th at about 13 years. After each dose the level rises, then falls. Approximate peaks: after the 1st dose, below about 0.1 IU/mL; after the 2nd, about 0.1; after the 3rd, about 1; after the 4th, about 5; after the 5th, about 10, after which the level levels off at about 1. Solid lines are labelled 'Immune'. Dashed lines run down into a shaded 'Non-immune' band at about 0.01 IU/mL and below.
prompts.hscSection: Section II (80 marks). Allow about 2 hours and 25 minutes for this section.

scenarioImage.alt: Line graph of tetanus antibody level against age at vaccination, showing five doses in the recommended schedule.

dotPoints.description: Compare pharmaceutical treatments for viral and bacterial diseases

prompts.question: Outline why antibiotics are not effective against viral infections.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 12 student is comparing treatments for a bacterial chest infection and for a viral cold. The student notes that antibiotics are prescribed for the bacterial infection but not for the cold.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines that antibiotics target structures or processes specific to bacteria, and that viruses lack these and replicate inside host cells
2 marks: Outlines that antibiotics target bacteria, and that viruses have different structures or replicate inside host cells
1 mark: Identifies that antibiotics are used for bacteria but not for viruses
markerNotes: Strong answers name a specific bacterial target, such as the peptidoglycan cell wall or the 70S ribosome, and then state that viruses lack it.
Credit the point that viruses use the host cell's machinery to replicate, so there is no separate viral process for the antibiotic to block.
Penalise answers that say antibiotics kill viruses more slowly, because the mechanism is missing.
commonStudentErrors: Says viruses are too small for antibiotics to reach, rather than explaining the missing target.
Says antibiotics do not work on viruses because viruses are dead.
Describes antibiotics as acting on the immune system rather than on the bacteria.

sampleAnswers.answer: Antibiotics act on structures or processes that are specific to bacteria, such as the peptidoglycan cell wall or the 70S ribosomes that make bacterial proteins. In a viral infection, the virus has no cell wall, no ribosomes of its own and no metabolism of its own, so there is no target for the antibiotic. Viruses replicate using the host cell's machinery, so an antibiotic cannot stop their replication without also harming the host.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: the bacterial targets are outlined and the virus lacks them, with the host-cell replication reason.

sampleAnswers.answer: Antibiotics target bacterial cell walls, but viruses do not have cell walls.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: outlines a bacterial target and a difference in virus structure, but not how viruses replicate.

sampleAnswers.answer: Antibiotics are used to treat bacterial infections.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: identifies the scope of antibiotics but gives no reason why they do not work on viruses.

prompts.question: Analyse why an antiviral drug, rather than an antibiotic, is the appropriate treatment for Patient 1, and why the reverse is true for Patient 2.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Patient 1 has a fever and sore throat, a nasal swab tests positive for influenza A virus, and symptoms began 36 hours ago. Patient 2 has a fever, productive cough and chest pain, and a sputum sample grows Streptococcus pneumoniae in culture.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses the mode of action of an antiviral and an antibiotic for each patient, with accurate reasons linked to the test results and the timing of treatment
5 marks: Analyses the treatment choice for both patients with mostly accurate mechanisms
4 marks: Describes the treatment choice for both patients with some reasons linked to the scenario
3 marks: Identifies a relevant drug for one patient with a limited reason
2 marks: Identifies an antiviral or antibiotic without linking it to a patient
1 mark: Identifies a relevant pathogen without a treatment
markerNotes: Strong answers name the target of each drug, such as the viral neuraminidase enzyme or the bacterial cell wall, and link it to the patient.
Credit the timing point for the antiviral, since oseltamivir is most effective when started early in the illness.
Credit a reference to antibiotic resistance as a reason to avoid antibiotics when they are not needed.
commonStudentErrors: Says the antiviral would kill the bacteria in Patient 2 as well as the virus in Patient 1.
Says antibiotics are appropriate for Patient 1 because the patient has a fever.
Describes oseltamivir as a vaccine rather than an antiviral drug.

sampleAnswers.answer: Patient 1 has a viral infection caused by influenza A virus, so an antibiotic would have no target and an antiviral drug is appropriate. Oseltamivir, an antiviral drug, inhibits neuraminidase, the viral enzyme that lets new virus particles leave infected cells, so it limits viral replication and spread. It is most effective when started within 48 hours of symptom onset, and Patient 1's 36 hours falls within that window. Patient 2 has a bacterial infection caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, which has a cell wall that antibiotics such as amoxicillin target. Amoxicillin blocks the synthesis of the peptidoglycan wall, so the growing bacterial cells weaken and burst. An antiviral drug would not act on the bacteria, so an antibiotic is appropriate for this bacterial infection. Prescribing antibiotics only when they are needed also reduces the selection of antibiotic resistance in bacteria.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row: each drug's target is analysed for the correct patient, with the timing of the antiviral and the resistance reason.

sampleAnswers.answer: Patient 1's influenza is a virus, so an antibiotic would have no target. Oseltamivir inhibits neuraminidase, which limits viral spread, and 36 hours falls within the window for treatment. Patient 2's Streptococcus pneumoniae has a cell wall, so an antibiotic is appropriate.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row: describes the treatment choice for both patients with reasons linked to the scenario, but the mechanisms are brief.

sampleAnswers.answer: Patient 1 has a virus, so an antiviral is needed. Patient 2 has bacteria, so an antibiotic is needed.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: identifies the drug type for each patient without explaining the target.

dotPoints.description: Describe the use of an Aboriginal bush medicine in treating disease

prompts.question: Describe how this Aboriginal bush medicine could help treat a skin infection.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Bundjalung family in northern New South Wales crushes fresh leaves of tea tree (Melaleuca alternifolia) and applies the crushed leaves to an infected cut. A student reads that oils from the leaves have shown antibacterial activity in laboratory tests.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes how the crushed leaves release antibacterial oils onto the wound, with a reason the compounds could reduce infection
2 marks: Describes how the preparation or application of the leaves could affect a skin infection, with limited reasoning
1 mark: Identifies tea tree or the crushed leaves without describing their effect
markerNotes: Strong answers link the preparation of the leaves to the release of the oils, and the oils to the effect on bacteria.
Credit careful wording that the oils are consistent with reducing infection, based on laboratory tests, rather than a claim that the medicine is proven.
Penalise answers that describe the family's knowledge as scientifically proven or as having no basis.
commonStudentErrors: Says the leaves cure the skin infection directly without any mechanism.
Describes the leaves as a food source for the bacteria.
Says the medicine works because it is traditional, rather than explaining the oils.

sampleAnswers.answer: This Aboriginal bush medicine may help a skin infection because crushing the tea tree leaves ruptures the oil glands, releasing oils such as terpinen-4-ol into the crushed leaves. Applied to the cut, the crushed leaves deliver these antibacterial oils, which may reduce bacterial growth in the wound. Laboratory tests show such activity, so the oils are consistent with helping the infection clear.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: the preparation and application are linked to the oils and to the reduction of bacteria, with careful wording about the evidence.

sampleAnswers.answer: Crushing the leaves releases oils, which are applied to the cut and may reduce bacteria.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: describes the preparation and application with a limited reason.

sampleAnswers.answer: Tea tree is an Australian native plant.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: identifies the plant without describing how it affects the infection.

prompts.question: Discuss the evidence needed before this bush medicine could be recommended as a treatment for an infected wound.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A researcher finds that an extract of tea tree leaves kills Staphylococcus aureus in a laboratory dish. No trial has yet tested the extract on people, and its concentration and safety on human skin are unknown. The Bundjalung family who use the leaves has not yet agreed to share their knowledge with the researcher.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Discusses the laboratory and clinical evidence needed on effectiveness, concentration and safety, and the need for consent and recognition of Aboriginal knowledge, reaching a supported judgement
5 marks: Discusses the need for laboratory and clinical evidence with reasoned links to effectiveness and safety
